articles.title: Evernote has laid off most of its US staff and will move most operations to Europe
articles.summary: Evernote parent company Bending Spoons said its layoff of most of its Chilean and US staff and shift to Europe would boost efficiency and take advantage of the Bending Spoons brand.
articles.body: Note-taking company Evernote has laid off most of its US- and- Chile-based employees, the company announced yesterday. Now Italian parent company Bending Spoons is taking most of Evernote’s operations to Europe. The company says the step is intended to “boost operational efficiency and to make the most of the Bending Spoons employer brand, which is extremely strong in Europe.” Bending Spoons acquired Evernote in November last year, and at the time, Evernote CEO was quoted as saying the deal would help the company work on building new features, using Bending Spoons’ “proven app expertise and wide range of proprietary technologies.” The company previously laid off 129 workers in February, with a Bending Spoons representative telling Tech Crunch at the time that the company’s unprofitable nature was “unsustainable in the long term.” Evernote said in its announcement yesterday that its employees were told on July 5th that the layoffs would happen, and has offered the employees 16 weeks of severance, a performance bonus, and up to a year’s worth of health insurance coverage. Evernote became one of the first popular note-taking apps when it launched in 2008, but has struggled since the mid-2010s as other, similar apps began to steal some of its thunder and the company has found itself bogged down in messes of its own making. After weathering complaints about it’s app’s bugginess and losing several executives, Evernote somehow made it out of its “death spiral” of 2016, a year in which it raised prices and was forced to renege on a controversial privacy policy that previously gave no option to opt out of employees looking at users’ content. We’ve reached out to both Evernote and Bending Spoons for comment.

articles.title: Bending Spoons confirmed it laid off all 22 of Filmic’s original staff
articles.summary: Bending Spoons quietly laid off the entire staff of video recording app Filmic last month and will develop the app with its own team going forward.
articles.body: Bending Spoons has laid off all of the staff behind mobile filmmaking app Filmic Pro, including Filmic CEO Neill Barham. Christy Keenan, a spokesperson for Bending Spoons, confirmed the layoffs in an email to The Verge, saying that “all 22 members of the original Filmic team” were laid off in November and Filmic “has now been fully integrated into the Bending Spoons platform.” PetaPixel first reported the layoffs on Friday. Keenan added that because the “dedicated team” at the company worked with Filmic’s original crew, it “possesses the necessary knowledge to ensure a seamless user experience.” The company was already involved in mobile video with its Splice video editing app, which it took over from GoPro in 2018. Bending Spoons bought Filmic in September 2022 and rolled out a $2.99 weekly subscription plan soon after (with a $50 per year option). That’s cheap for a professional app, but Filmic Pro’s previous one-time payment system made it much more accessible for independent filmmakers. Bending Spoons has made similar changes for Evernote, another company it bought last year before laying off most of its original staff over the summer. Filmic Pro enjoyed plenty of popularity among mobile filmmakers over the years, having been used to shoot movies and music videos. Apple even featured the Filmic DoubleTake dual-camera recording app prominently when it overhauled its camera approach for the iPhone 11 Pro phones. Filmic even announced FilmicFest 2023, its annual competitive mobile filmmaking festival, would return this year with a $25,000 grand prize, but that’s presumably canceled since the event signup page no longer exists. Some former high-level employees posted about their departure. Christopher Cohen, who was Filmic’s technical chief officer, posted on November 3rd that he was no longer with the company. Kevin Buonagurio, the company’s now-former chief operating officer, replied to a LinkedIn user who’d shared the PetaPixel story yesterday, saying that “pushing the envelope” of mobile filmmaking was part of “what made the Filmic journey so fulfilling for us.” Update December 4th, 2023, 9:57AM ET: Added confirmation from Bending Spoons spokesperson Christy Keenan.

articles.title: Charlie Sheen’s “Frightening” Last Days on Two and a Half Men Revealed
articles.summary: Two and a Half Men creator Chuck Lorre described Charlie Sheen’s final days on set amid his 2011 public downfall as a “scary time” during an exclusive interv...
articles.body:
Charlie Sheen wasn't winning when his time on Two and a Half Men came to an abrupt end.

In fact, in the lead up to his firing from the series at the height of his public meltdown in 2011, Chuck Lorre admitted the energy around the set was "dark" and "frightening."

"I think I can speak for everyone who was working on the show back then that we were frightened that something terrible was going to happen," the sitcom co-creator told E! News in an exclusive interview. "We were frightened that Charlie might get hurt, that someone else might get hurt."

Indeed, the legendary showrunner—also creator of The Big Bang Theory and Mike & Molly —emphasized that his concern for Sheen at the time was "no longer about misbehavior," and instead focused on everyone's safety.

"This was about our people, including our friend and the star of the show, physically in danger and people around them would be in danger," he continued. "So, it was a scary, scary time, and it took me many years to put it in perspective."

In his new memoir Sitcom: A Memoir by Chuck Lorre , on shelves Oct. 13, Lorre recalled how the show had begun to "unravel" in Sheen's final season and that the cast and crew "worked in a constant state of anxiety."

Eventually, the chaos culminated in the actor's final scene on the series, which also featured Melanie Lynskey .

"He couldn't remember any of his lines and had to use the furniture to keep himself upright," Lorre wrote, per an excerpt published by Vanity Fair . "Melanie was terrified. It was clear to everyone that this man, whom we'd all grown to love, was in trouble. I had no choice but to shut down the show."

With time, Lorre was able to overcome Sheen's antics, which included the actor writing an open letter in 2011 calling his boss a "maggot" and wishing him "pain." (Sheen is now nine years sober and has shared candidly about his sobriety journey.)

And the pair even proved they had mended their relationship when Lorre cast Sheen as a heightened version of himself in the 2023 gambling-centric show Bookie starring Sebastian Maniscalco .

"[My co-creator] Nick [ Bakay ] said, 'Can you work with him?' Which is a legitimate question. It didn't end very well with he and I," he explained to E!. "And I said, 'I'm actually in a good place right now. And if he's in a good place, I'd be fine with it.'"

So, Lorre "simply called him." And the Wall Street star was just as game to move past the bad blood.

"He was to the best of my knowledge in a very good place in his life right now, that madness is in the rearview mirror," he shared. "And we had a blast. We did a couple episodes of Bookie with Sebastian Maniscalco, and he killed it. He was hilarious at playing himself with a serious gambling problem."

articles.title: All the news from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
articles.summary: Apple is hosting a “Welcome home” event on October 13th that seems like it will be about the smart home, and you can follow our coverage right here.
articles.body: Apple’s October 13th launch event — given the tagline “Welcome Home” — is all about its efforts for the smart home. The event was headlined by the debut of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart home display. It also launched a collection of smart home devices, including cameras, thermostats, and a smart lock, in partnership with other companies. On top of the new device categories, Apple also refreshed two familiar ones. The HomePod Mini 2 was announced with support for Siri AI, and the Apple TV 4K also received a Siri AI-focused refresh. You can follow along with all of our coverage right here.

articles.title: Apple announces the HomePod Mini 2, but it isn’t ready for Siri AI at launch
articles.summary: The new speaker can sync its lights with your album art and pair with the new Apple TV and HomePods for a home theatre setup.
articles.body: Apple is announcing the long-awaited HomePod Mini 2 with a new chip that can power Siri AI — but support for those new AI features won’t be available at launch. The speaker is also getting a new sound glow feature that syncs its LED lights with a song’s album art, and it can now be your Mac’s default speaker. Up to four can also pair with the new Apple TV 4K for surround sound. And like everything this year, it’s more expensive, too. The HomePod Mini 2 comes in pink, green, and a new shade of blue, along with white and black. It costs $149, $20 more than its predecessor, which is being discontinued. Preorders open today, October 13th, and it will ship on October 30th. Apple announced the smart speaker alongside a suite of new products for the home, including the new HomeView smart display ($299), the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K ($299), and a new collection of smart home devices developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric starting at $199. [Image: The HomePod Mini 2 in pink. The biggest upgrade inside the HomePod Mini 2 is the S10 chip, which debuted in the Apple Watch Series 10 in 2024. Here, it will enable Siri AI and bring smarter, more conversational responses to the speaker. However, the Mini 2 won’t ship with Siri AI at launch; instead, Apple says it will arrive in a later software update. It will be available in English in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and India. You’ll need an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone — an iPhone 15 Pro or newer — to enable the upgrade. Once upgraded, you’ll get the same Siri AI as on compatible iPhones, capable of understanding natural language commands and accessing what Apple calls “broader world knowledge,” as well as your personal context, such as your calendar and text messages. Apple’s examples include: if you ask Siri to set a reminder to buy flowers for mom’s birthday, it can check your calendar, identify when mom’s birthday is, and set the reminder. It can also scan your text messages for music recommendations so you can ask it to play that song your friend sent. [Video: Apple HomePod Mini 2 Sound Glow] Personal context will be available only on the Mini if you have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, and will rely on voice recognition to keep your personal information private, but anyone in the home can talk to the HomePod to ask questions, play music, and control most smart home devices. Apple confirmed that Siri AI will not be coming to existing HomePod Minis. The speakers don’t appear to have been upgraded from the original Mini, with Apple saying they offer the same great sound, but they do get three new audio features: sound glow, audio companion capability for your Mac, and surround sound support on the new Apple TV 4K. [Media: Sound glow matches the colors of a song’s album art with the LEDs on top of the speaker. I saw a demo in a brightly lit room, and it was subtle, but the colors clearly changed in sync with the music. It also works with Apple’s ambient soundscapes, such as rain, forest, and ocean sounds. The Mini 2 can now serve as your Mac’s default speaker and work as a surround-sound pair with the new Apple TV 4K, also announced today for $299. The new colors match a few of the current iMacs; I saw the pink pairing, and it was very pretty. Apple says the Mini uses a new audio companion feature that enables a persistent AirPlay setup and optimizes the streaming architecture for low-latency, responsive sound. It works on any model that supports Wi-Fi 6E or higher. I saw a demo of Angry Birds and the fruit-flinging on screen synced seamlessly with the splat sounds emanating from two Minis. [Image: Some of the HomePod Mini 2 colors match the current iMac line. You can pair two as the default speakers for your Mac. You’ll be able to pair up to four of the Mini 2 speakers with the new Apple TV 4K for a surround sound home theatre setup. Two Minis can also work with a pair of the second-gen full-sized HomePods for fuller sound. Apple says the speakers automatically calibrate with the Apple TV 4K to understand where they are in the room and relative to each other, then tune the audio levels to fit the space. The first-generation HomePod Mini launched six years ago today, so a full upgrade was long overdue. The jump from the S5 chip the OG Mini ran on to the S10, and the bump up to Wi-Fi 6E and BLE 6.0, should also improve speed and responsiveness. It’s disappointing that the Mini hasn’t gotten a significant audio upgrade, but the addition of a smarter Siri, when it arrives, should make the speaker more useful at home. However, it’s surprising that Apple launched this without Siri AI, meaning even if you spend $149 on a new Mini, you’ll still have a disconnect between Siri on your phone and Siri in your home. Combined with the fact that Siri AI is in beta on the new Apple TV 4K, it sounds like Apple’s smart voice assistant isn’t quite ready for primetime after all.

articles.title: The new Apple TV 4K has built-in microphones so you can talk to Siri AI
articles.summary: The fourth-gen streaming box also gets a surround-sound upgrade and the ability to find your Siri remote.
articles.body: Apple is introducing a refreshed Apple TV 4K today with a pair of interesting new hardware features: far-field microphones to talk to Siri hands-free and Find My built into the remote. The fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, announced at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, is the first model to support the Siri AI voice assistant and has a new home theatre feature that lets you pair up to four second-gen HomePods or HomePod Mini 2s for surround sound. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299, more than twice the price the prior-generation Apple TV 4K debuted at and $50 more than the current top-of-the-line model (which is being discontinued). The fourth-gen model matches that version’s specs with 128GB of storage, an Ethernet port, and support for Thread and Matter, but it’s getting a bump up to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. It will be available on November 13th, with preorders opening today, October 13th. [Video: Apple TV 4K far field microphones] Apple announced the device as part of a major new push into the smart home, which includes the new HomeView smart display ($299), HomePod Mini 2 ($149), and a collection of smart home devices developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The new Apple TV comes with an A19 chip, first seen in last year’s iPhone 17, which adds Siri AI support out of the box. It will launch in beta and be available in English in eight countries — the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and India. Apple says Siri AI lets you use natural language to talk to the voice assistant through the remote or the new microphones and ask for recommendations, such as “What are the best nature docs on Apple TV right now?” [Media: Unlike on the HomePod or HomeView, Siri doesn’t speak its responses aloud on Apple TV; they appear either full screen when you search for content or in a text bubble when you ask general knowledge questions. In the demo I saw, someone asked if the soccer team we were watching in an episode of Ted Lasso was real, and Siri displayed a few sentences answering the query (no, it’s fictional) that covered the top-right corner of the screen. We’ve already seen AI-powered search features on Google’s TV Streamer with Gemini and Amazon’s Fire TV with Alexa Plus, but Apple is taking its streaming box’s AI capabilities further with the addition of personal context. Personal context uses information from your Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, so you can say “Play that show my friend texted me,” and it will pull from your text messages and find what you were sent. [Image: The Apple TV 4K can pair with up to four compatible HomePod speakers for surround sound. The group of four consists of two pairs, and each pair must use comparable speakers. The design of the streaming box and its remote hasn’t changed, but the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K now supports an expanded surround-sound setup. You can use four compatible HomePod speakers in pairs, up from the two you can use with current Apple TV models. Compatible speakers include the HomePod second-gen and the HomePod Mini 2, also announced today for $149. There are three available configurations: four HomePod second-gens, four HomePod Mini 2s, or a pair of HomePod second-gens and a pair of HomePod Mini 2s. The feature is exclusive to the new Apple TV 4K, and Apple says the speakers automatically calibrate with the device to understand where they are in the room and relative to each other, then tune the audio levels to fit the space. I’m most excited to be able to say “Hey Siri, can you find the remote?” Apple has finally added Find My to the Siri Remote. It can now play that familiar ringing sound so you can find which cushion it’s fallen under. If for some reason you can’t hear it, you can now use the Find My app on your iPhone to track its precise location, thanks to Apple adding support for Bluetooth channel sounding, a location technology similar to ultra-wideband, but without the need for a UWB chip.

articles.title: Everything Apple launched at its ‘Welcome Home’ event
articles.summary: Apple has unveiled a slate of new smart home gadgets, including its first smart home hub, new security cameras, and updated Apple TV and HomePod devices.
articles.body: Apple unveiled a slate of new smart home gadgets at its aptly named “Welcome Home” event today, including its first (and highly anticipated) smart home hub. That flagship announcement came alongside much-needed refreshes for Apple’s HomePod Mini and TV 4K devices, and a selection of new smart home and security accessories designed together with trusted third-party manufacturers. Catch up on all of Apple’s new hardware announcements in our roundup below, or click through for more detailed coverage on each. The HomeView is Apple’s first smart display [Image: [Image: HomeView is arguably the company’s first major Apple Home launch since releasing HomeKit in 2014. It gives you a dedicated display to monitor and control compatible smart home gadgets and security devices around your living space — something that Amazon and Google have long offered for their own smart home platforms in the form of Echo Show and Nest Hub devices. The $299 HomeView is available in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. It features a 7-inch, square-shaped, Liquid Retina display on a rounded speaker base (or it can be wall-mounted), in a design reminiscent of Apple’s 2002 iMac G4. The HomeView display can automatically adjust light levels to suit its surroundings, and can be dimmed down to just 0.3 nits of brightness so it can comfortably sit on your nightstand without blinding you at night. A 12-megapixel camera can be used for FaceTime calls, and enables the device to recognize up to six different users — automatically adapting from a shared household screen to a personalized hub when perception and recognition features are enabled. Feature-wise, HomeView has all the usual smart home hub capabilities you’d expect: you can manage lighting, thermostat, and other smart device controls, and monitor a live view of up to nine security cameras. There are also some Apple Intelligence-powered Siri AI features such as personal context and text descriptions for video feeds, but these are leveraged via an iPhone connection. In fact, HomeView requires every user in a household to have an iPhone with the latest OS, which may cause problems in mixed iOS / Android households, or for anyone with an older iPhone. It’s available to preorder today, with availability starting from November 13th. The HomePod Mini gets a refresh [Image: The glowing ball is back, this time in more muted colors. We’ve been expecting Apple to drop a refreshed version of its petite pod speaker since sparse details leaked in September, but now the update is official. The $149 HomePod Mini 2 is $50 more than the debut price of its six-year-old predecessor and retains many of the same design features, but it’s still cheaper than the larger second-gen HomePod, which launched in 2023 at $299. It has the same familiar ball shape, but the previously vivid color options are more muted: pink, blue, green, white, and midnight, color-matched with the current iMac models. The colorful lighting swirl on the top panel also makes a reappearance, but Apple has upgraded it with a “sound glow” feature that matches the illumination to the color of album cover art and other pretty soundscape designs. The HomePod Mini 2 is powered by the same S10 chip that’s found inside the Apple Watch Series 10, and includes support for WiFi 6E, Bluetooth 6, and both Thread and Matter. Support for Siri AI via a connected iPhone will be coming in a “later” software update, according to Apple. It can be used as the default speaker for your Mac, and multiple speakers can be connected together to provide a surround sound experience: either four HomePod Mini 2 speakers, or two second-gen HomePods with two HomePod Mini 2s. The HomePod Mini 2 can also automatically calibrate with the new Apple TV 4K to understand where the devices are positioned in the room, and relative to each other, tuning audio to best match the space. You can preorder the new HomePod Mini 2 today, with shipping starting on October 30th. The new Apple TV 4K comes with built-in mics [Image: The new Apple TV 4K doesn’t change much in its design, but now it comes with built-in microphones. This is the fourth generation of Apple’s TV hardware, and comes with some minor but appreciated quality-of-life upgrades compared to its predecessor, released in 2022. The new Apple TV 4K is $299 and comes with four far-field microphones built into the set-top box — meaning you no longer have to speak into the remote or a connected HomePod device to control it via Siri. It doesn’t respond out loud, however, so any answers will be displayed as on-screen text. You can also pair the new Apple TV 4K with a compatible iPhone to use Siri AI features, such as leveraging personal context to surface a TV series suggested by a friend over text messages, and asking the AI assistant to recommend shows to watch on Apple TV (the streaming service, not the device). If you lose your remote, you can ask Siri to locate it using Bluetooth Channel Sounding and make it play a sound. Preorders are available starting today, with shipping expected on November 13th. Home Collection features smart home gadgets from LG and Schneider Electric [Image: These smart home gadgets are built by partner companies, but they still have that “Apple” look to them. Apple also announced a new range of smart home hardware, designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The Apple Home Collection includes multiple cameras from LG: a $199 indoor camera that automatically tilts down when you arrive home to provide some personal privacy, a $299 outdoor security camera with optional motion-activated floodlights (raising the price to $399), and a $249 video doorbell. These are all HomeKit Secure Video cameras, meaning they can detect people, pets, packages, and vehicles, and support Apple Intelligence features via a connected iPhone. The collection also includes an LG door lock and two thermostats — one from LG and the other made by Schneider. All of the listed devices use NFC and are designed to be set up easily, similar to the experience of pairing AirPods. Just approach them with your iPhone, follow the on-screen steps, and the device is automatically added to your Home app. Apple hasn’t mentioned a release date for this smart home gadget collection, only that it’s “coming soon.” Correction, October 13th: This story initially misstated the price of the new Apple TV 4K. It is $299, not $149.

articles.title: Apple makes another push into the smart home market with HomeView | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple is taking a big swing at the smart home market with its latest product that competes with Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub.
articles.body:
Apple is taking a big swing at the smart home market. The company on Tuesday unveiled its long-rumored smart home hub, dubbed HomeView, that can act as a central control point for smart home devices, be used for FaceTime calls, playing music, watching videos, displaying photo slideshows, and more.

The new $299 device looks like a cuboid version of the HomePod, but with a display added to the front. The HomeView comes in two versions: one can sit on a countertop, and the other can be mounted on a wall. Measuring 7 inches wide, the hub features a single FaceTime camera on the front, and has microphones and speakers built into its base.

Apple has preloaded the device with several of its apps, including Calendar, Messages, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music, and Podcasts. That means users won’t need to reach for their iPhone if they want to check a calendar appointment, send a message, play some music, or look at photos.

Apple sees the device being particularly useful in places such as the kitchen. Someone cooking dinner, for example, could pull up a recipe, watch a video, check a calendar, or start a FaceTime call without resorting to their phone.

It’ll also act as a smart home dashboard, allowing users to ask Siri to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, turn on lights, and lock doors. This comes as Apple announced its lineup of smart home accessories today, including a smart deadbolt lock, security cameras, and doorbell. Users will hear a chime from their HomeView when someone is at the door, for example.

One of the more interesting aspects of the device is how it works with different members of a household.

The hub runs Apple’s updated Siri AI assistant and can recognize individual people in the house. Once it identifies someone, the screen can show information meant for that person, such as their messages, contacts, calendar appointments, notes, and preferred apps. The experience changes automatically when another family member walks up to the device.

The company says HomeView can recognize up to six people.

HomeView puts Apple in a much more direct fight with Amazon and Google, both of which already have established smart display products: Amazon has its Echo Show line, while Google offers the Nest Hub.

Apple has had a mixed history in the smart home space, however, with products such as the HomePod struggling to reach the same level of popularity as competing devices. The new hub is an opportunity for Apple to change that by combining home controls with the company’s wider ecosystem.

The device has been rumored for quite some time, with reports pointing to delays caused in part by problems with Siri AI. Those issues have reportedly affected Apple’s broader smart home plans as well.

This may only be the first phase of Apple’s smart home plan. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has previously reported that Apple could eventually take the concept further with a more advanced version that features a robotic arm. Such a device could move its display and interact in a more physical way.

Preorders start today, and the device will be available to buy from November 13. It comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray.

articles.title: Apple launches a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI and remote-free voice commands | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new Apple TV 4K costs $299, comes with Siri AI, and will be available on November 13.
articles.body:
Apple launched a new $299 Apple TV 4K streaming device today, with an upgraded chip, integration with the updated version of Siri AI for content discovery, and mics that allow users to issue voice commands directly without using the remote.

The refreshed Apple TV 4K comes with an upgraded A19 chip to enable various AI features. Hardware-wise, the new streaming box comes with three far-field microphones, letting users talk with Siri without a remote or a paired HomePod.

The company said that users can now have a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2 speakers.

The remote also gets a welcome update: It now includes a small speaker. This helps users find the remote easily when it gets lost in the nooks and corners of the couch or when they leave the remote in another room while doing a chore. (Apple added a way to find the remote with Siri and Find My in 2023 , but it hinged on showing directions in the app rather than an audible sound.)

With Siri AI now rolling out to all Apple platforms, the big draw for Apple is to utilize it for better personalization and content recommendations. On the Apple TV, viewers can ask questions like “Which Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” to search for content, or ask for more information about shows with questions like “Where was ‘Pluribus’ filmed?”

Rivals Google and Amazon have also added AI for content suggestions in the past few years.

The device is not updated as often as other Apple hardware, given this long-pending upgrade comes four years after the launch of Apple TV 4K in 2022. Bloomberg reported that the company wanted to launch the new device in 2024, but delays in launching the AI-powered Siri forced Apple to push the launch of new home devices as well.

Consumers can preorder the new Apple TV 4K starting today, and the device will be available on November 13.

articles.title: Apple's new smart home lineup includes a smart lock, thermostat, and video doorbells | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new devices work with HomeView, the company's new smart home hub which can be used to control accessories and interact with apps.
articles.body:
Apple is getting serious about the smart home space. The company on Tuesday showed off its new Apple Home Collection, which includes a new smart deadbolt lock, video doorbell, thermostat, temperature sensor, and a range of security cameras.

The new devices are designed to work with HomeView , the company’s new smart home hub which can be used to control connected accessories and interact with Apple’s software.

This new range of smart home accessories could help Apple compete better with Amazon Ring and Google Nest, two established players in connected home security. The products will become available in December.

Apple says the devices were built in partnership with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric — an interesting move for the company, which has long sought to build and support every smart home accessory itself.

The smart lock, priced at $349.95, stands out for its support for ultra-wideband (UWB), a wireless technology that enables more precise proximity detection than traditional Bluetooth. This could allow the lock to recognize when an authorized user approaches and automatically unlock the door, reducing the need to pull out a phone or reach for a physical key.

The $249.95 wired video doorbell, meanwhile, will let homeowners see who’s outside, monitor visitors, and receive notifications when someone approaches their property. When someone rings it, a chime will sound through Apple devices like HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini. Users will also be notified on their iPhone or iPad.

As for the temperature sensor, it can provide insight into conditions in individual rooms, helping users identify temperature differences between areas and make adjustments.

For security, Apple is also introducing indoor and outdoor cameras, as well as a floodlight camera ($399.95) that combines exterior lighting with video monitoring. The camera lineup includes features such as live viewing, motion detection, intelligent alerts, and video storage.

articles.title: Apple refreshes its HomePod mini with a new chip and $149 price tag | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new $149 HomePod mini with Siri AI and a 'SoundGlow' visual feature will be available starting October 30.
articles.body:
Apple’s new HomeView device was the center of the show at its smart home event on Tuesday, but the company also refreshed its HomePod mini smart speaker with a new chip and Siri AI integration, the latter of which will be available through a future update.

The $149 update is $50 more expensive than the original version launched over six years ago in 2020 . The new HomePod mini has an S10 chip that helps improve optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance.

With the new HomePod mini, users can control their smart home devices through voice commands. Plus, the speaker can listen for sounds like a smoke alarm and send a notification to users’ phones — a feature that Alexa devices have offered for years.

Apple said that with Siri AI, users will be able to have multi-turn conversations, but it didn’t provide a date for when the new assistant will be available to HomePod mini 2 buyers.

The company also said the new speaker works better with its other devices. For instance, users could form a four-speaker home entertainment system paired with the new Apple TV 4K . Plus, the HomePod mini 2 speakers can be the default speaker for Mac for video calls or music playback instead of built-in speakers.

The device has another new feature, as well: a visual canvas called “Sound Glow,” which uses the color scheme of the album art to turn the top of the HomePod mini into a visual canvas that will glow and pulse in sync with the music. Users can also pick soundscapes like rain or ocean waves to start animations.

The new speaker comes in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight colorways and will be available starting October 30. Consumers can preorder starting today.

articles.title: Buying Apple’s wall-mounted HomeView? The mount costs extra
articles.summary: The wall mounted version of Apple’s HomeView smart display hub requires you to pay at least $60 more to include the wall mount itself.
articles.body: The HomeView smart home display announced by Apple today comes in two models that both cost $299: one with a speaker base, and the other being a self explanatory “Wall Mounted” version. If you want the latter, however, you’ll actually have to pay at least $59 more — the mounts required to actually affix the display to your wall are sold separately. Maybe calling it the “Mountless” version would have been more accurate? Apple isn’t exactly shouting about that sneaky additional premium for wall-mounted HomeView customers. The details are mentioned in the small print at the bottom of the product announcement page: > HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (US), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (US), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (US). It also becomes apparent when you go through the process of adding the HomeView to your basket on Apple’s webstore. You’re asked to choose from the available mount options (which doesn’t include the Power Mount PoE Wired yet) which each bump up that $299 price, or select “No mount” to proceed with no extra charge — but Apple clearly states on this option that the “HomeView (Wall Mounted) requires a mount and power solution to operate.” [Image: Given you don’t get the funky iMac G4-style speaker base, it feels like Apple is charging the same price for half the product. Given it doesn’t ship with a power source, you can’t have the wall model HomeView leaning against something or laying on a flat surface to evade the extra cost. You also can’t buy the desktop model that doesn’t have any additional requirements and keep the speaker base aside because it can’t be converted into the wall version. They’re two distinct versions, and the wall option only comes in two colors. Presumably some third-party manufacturers will release more affordable wall mount options in time, but either way, folks who want to wall mount their HomeView will pay a premium over those who opt for the desktop model.

articles.title: I tried out Apple’s HomeView smart display
articles.summary: Apple just revealed the HomeView — its first smart home display — and we got to try it out.
articles.body: Apple has just announced the HomeView, its first smart home display — and I just got hands-on with the device, which features a gorgeous 7-inch square touchscreen and built-in Siri AI. It’s designed as a smart home controller, personal assistant, and home hub for your household, so there was a lot to check out. [Image: The HomeView has a 12MP camera for FaceTime, facial recognition, and quick makeup checks (that’s me with the orange phone!). The first thing that struck me about the HomeView was its size. It’s much smaller than I expected, and the screen almost entirely hides the small aluminum base that acts as a speaker. The Liquid Retina display is bright and responsive to touch, and it displays photos and the HomeView “faces” brilliantly. You can swipe to change faces easily and choose from dozens of options, most of which resemble Apple Watch faces. The display feels like a giant Apple Watch paired with the functionality of an iPhone and the room to breathe of an iPad. [Media: Apple offers both a wall-mounted and tabletop version of the HomeView, and the wall-mounted model looks like it will make a great smart home controller. A dedicated Home Widget face pulls devices from the Apple Home app; I could walk up and tap to control a thermostat and door lock and activate a scene, or I could swipe right to get a live view of HomeKit Secure Video cameras and tap into one to access nearby accessories, such as opening the garage door. When I tried to unlock a door, it stopped me, asking me to authenticate with my face or iPhone. [Image: [Image: The Home Widget is a skin of the Home app, so it offers all the controls you have with that app on your iPhone, just on a bigger screen designed for walk-up-and-tap interaction. There’s a lot of swiping on the HomeView. Swipe left to get to new home faces, tap widgets to access deeper controls in apps, then swipe right for more features. You swipe up to return to the main screen, then up again to access the onboard apps, which automatically populate from your phone. Swiping down from the top of the screen brings up a control center, just like on an iPhone. You can even enable the 12MP camera from here, giving you a de facto mirror. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The HomeView is built around Siri AI, and it can pull personal context such as text messages and calendar appointments based on voice requests. I didn’t get to try this myself, but saw a demo where it was asked what time Andrew would arrive from the airport, pulling context together to take actions: “Hey, Siri, what time did Andrew say he’s getting in from JFK?” Siri: Andrew Dean sent a message saying his flight lands at JFK Airport at 6:30AM on October 16th. “How long will it take him to get to my place if he takes the train from JFK? Okay, I know he didn’t pack any bags.” Siri: It will take about 1 hour and eight minutes to get from JFK to your place by transit. “Okay, let’s turn on the coffee maker 15 minutes before he’ll arrive.” Siri: Sets a routine to turn on the coffee maker at the correct time. This integration of your personal context with the smart home, all orchestrated by the HomeView, is a big jump up in capability for Apple Home, and I’m looking forward to testing it myself. [Image: The iPhone handing off a recipe to the HomeView. One of my favorite features, being a big home chef, is the guided cooking experience on the HomeView. You can bring your iPhone, with a recipe pulled up in Siri, to the screen, and it will use Handoff to transfer the data, then reformat the recipe into an easy-to-follow onscreen experience, complete with in-line timers for each step. Apple says most recipes that use Google formatting will work this way. I’m wondering how it will handle TikTok recipes. Another Siri AI demo had the user asking Siri to play that song her friend texted, and it started playing Bad Bunny. It took about eight seconds to pull up the song, but considering what it was doing, that felt fairly fast. I also saw a FaceTime demo where we were centered on the screen thanks to Center Stage, and I see this as a great countertop calling device. I only got to try a few HomeView features today, but I’m looking forward to testing more soon. It costs $299 and is available for preorder today. It starts shipping on November 13th. articles.title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google is making it easier to build and use personal Android apps created with AI, without having to make them available to everyone on the Play Store.
articles.body:
Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private.

These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator.

The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android.

Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use.

These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android.

Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up.

“That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.”

In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store.

And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews.

Related to AI’s impact on app development, Google said it’s also building better ways to curate the Google Play experience — for instance, by leveraging Google’s AI to create a personalized game recommendation engine, called Game Finder. The feature, first available in the U.S. in English, will be based on what the user likes to play combined with Google’s knowledge derived from its game community’s 1.2 billion players.

Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates.

Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations.

The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience.

articles.title: The Xteink X4 Pro is a great, tiny e-reader, and it’s cheaper than ever
articles.summary: Xteink’s X4 Pro is down to a new low price of $84.15 ($25 off) at Amazon. Along with a pocketable design, it features a touchscreen and built-in lighting.
articles.body: If you’re looking for an e-reader that can easily fit in your pocket (or snap onto your magnet-equipped phone), the tiny Xteink X4 Pro might be worth a look. It features a 4.26-inch, 800 x 480 E Ink display, making it significantly smaller and thinner than Amazon’s smallest six-inch Kindle. It’s also quite a bit cheaper. Right now, you can pick it up for $84.15 ($25 off) at Amazon, which is its best price to date. [Product: Xteink X4 Pro | The X4 Pro brings several welcome upgrades over its predecessors, including a touchscreen that gives readers another way to interact with it. It still has physical page-turning buttons, though. There’s also a new touch-sensitive button below the display for quickly returning to the home screen, along with a built-in light with adjustable brightness and color temperature, so you can read in the dark. It ships with the excellent CrossPoint Reader software, which makes navigating your library and reading books a much better experience than on previous Xteink models we’ve tested, though it’s still not quite as polished as Amazon’s software. Understandably, not everyone is a fan of Xteink’s decision to swap the X4 Pro’s USB-C port for a proprietary charging connector. If you can look past that, the X4 Pro is a great, little e-reader that features magnets that let you attach it to compatible smartphones, just like previous models. The magnetic connection is stronger this time around, though we still wish it were a little more secure. All the same, my colleague Andrew Liszewski still considers the X4 Pro the best tiny e-reader you can buy, calling it a device he “won’t leave the house without.” Read our hands-on impressions.

articles.title: The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
articles.summary: Federal safety regulator NHTSA is weighing whether to open an investigation over reports that Tesla’s Model Y and Cybercab robotaxis are violating school zone speed limits.
articles.body: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s evaluating allegations that Tesla’s 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding “posted speed limits in active school zones.” Waymo’s robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including for illegally passing school buses and hitting a child near a California elementary school. articles.title: I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
articles.summary: The $349 Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses can’t record video and are a decent pair of open-ear headphones. But they don’t solve the privacy problem.
articles.body: The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.” These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep. [Product: Ray-Ban Meta Audio | The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware. Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you. You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.) [Image: You can see the small, customizable action button on the right-hand temple arm. I programmed it to bring up Meta AI so I don’t have to say “Hey Meta” in public. I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started. I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much. At least, not yet. Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning. [Image: Without a camera, the temple arms are much thinner, too. For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else. Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings. I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses. So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones. I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance. Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it. [Image: You can’t really tell that these are smart glasses unless you look really closely at the transparent portion of the arms. At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than every other pair of Meta glasses I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit. I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs. Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays without sticking the glasses back into the case. Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of not worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off. But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses. [Image: This is me wondering how my beat went from tracking steps to discussing wearable surveillance and hoping bystanders won’t punch me. I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I don’t think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who would miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option. Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort for now. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables, the definition of recording, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our lives. Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Ray-Ban Meta Audio Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, you’ll need a Meta account and the Meta AI app downloaded onto your phone. A Meta account works across platforms like Meta, Instagram, and Quest and comes with its own terms of service and privacy policy. Should you decide to integrate with services like WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, Apple Music, Apple Health, Garmin, Strava, Amazon Music, and Spotify, you also agree to those terms and privacy policies. You may also be asked to give permissions related to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, location services, and voice data. If you choose to get a pair of prescription lenses, you may also be asked to share that information with Ray-Ban and/or LensCrafters. If you are concerned about privacy, you can access the Glasses Privacy menu in the glasses’ settings. There you can view the voice activity log as well as the “Share additional data” toggle. To access the visual data opt-out toggle, go to the glasses’ settings and navigate to the Meta AI menu. The smart glasses also come with supplemental terms of service and privacy policies / notices, including: * Supplemental Meta Platforms Technologies Terms of Service * Supplemental Meta Platforms Technologies Privacy Policy * Meta AI app terms * Meta AI glasses privacy settings * United States Regional Privacy Notice * Health and Safety Information * Voice Controls Privacy Notice * Meta AI Third-Party Notices Final tally: Two mandatory agreements, eight supplemental agreements and notices, and several optional agreements.

articles.title: Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
articles.summary: Mind Robotics, founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe, announced the appointment of Doug Field as president. Field worked at Tesla, Apple, and most recently Ford, running the automaker’s EV and software division.
articles.body: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project. Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year. Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work. “Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.” Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions. Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots. Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup. “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.” Correction October 13th: Mind Robotics is a partner of Rivian, but not a spinoff. A previous version of this story misstated the relationship between the companies.

articles.title: Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
articles.summary: Zelenskyy celebrated ‘less division’ on social media after the strikes but the data isn’t backing that up yet.
articles.body: Days after Ukrainian military drones took down several Russian data centers, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that the campaign had hurt Russia’s disinformation efforts. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms,” Zelenskyy said Monday. “There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations.” Zelenskyy isn’t the first to assert that the drone operation, which targeted data centers belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex, has cut down on spam and disinformation campaigns fomented by Russian bot farms. Social media users have claimed they’ve noticed less traffic on posts by MAGA-affiliated accounts, as well as those associated with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Some have even said they’ve noticed a steep drop in spam calls and messages. [Media: But these people are wrong. The drone strikes appear to have affected Yandex’s web crawlers, not any disinformation or political operations. In fact, the account antibot4navalny, which tracks state-sponsored troll farms, reports that bot traffic is steady as ever. On Monday, the same day Zelenskyy claimed that disinformation had died down, antibot4navalny reported that several Kremlin-aligned accounts posted videos falsely claiming that experts are demanding the European Union lift the ongoing sanctions on Russia. Danish analyst Valdemar Osted said interactions on MAGA and AfD accounts have actually increased since the strikes. And the charts purportedly showing a decline in bot activity appear to be AI-generated. Ironically, claims that the drone strikes hindered Russian disinformation campaigns appears to be a form of disinformation itself, no matter what Zelenskyy says.

articles.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech's most expensive mistakes | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The San Francisco startup aims to help battery and chip manufacturers identify defects on production lines, reducing downtime and costly mistakes.
articles.body:
San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days.

How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause.

Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines.

Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today.

“It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.”

“Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha.

Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model.

“None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data.

Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid).

He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers.

If you’re curious to learn more, Niobia will present onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt this afternoon in San Francisco. Join us to catch the company and the 19 startups against which it’s competing as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, happening today, Tuesday, through Thursday, October 15.
